title: Inference network-aware batching and routing IaC design
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary

This design and runbook describes a cross-cutting infrastructure pattern used by Redwood to implement network-aware request batching and smart routing for inference workloads. It ties together GPU fleet placement, VPC/egress controls, Terraform modules, and CI/CD gating so that inference requests are batched and routed based on network path health, tenant locality, and GPU pool characteristics. The goal is to lower tail latency and egress cost while preserving SLOs and simplifying operator response during network incidents.

Why this exists

- Inference exhibits sensitivity to both GPU packing and inter-service network performance (KV cache fetches, feature service calls).
- Naive batching can amplify network spikes (large batches waiting on slow cross-region RPCs).
- We need an automated, auditable IaC pattern that ties routing policy to network telemetry and deploys compatible batching profiles per route.

Intended audience

- Infra engineers operating GPU fleets and network egress
- Platform engineers owning the inference control plane
- SREs responsible for SLOs and incident response

Design overview

1) Key concepts

- Network-aware batching profile: a small JSON object defining batch size, max latency, KV cache warmup thresholds, and a preferred egress path tag.
- Routing policy controller: a control-plane service that maps incoming routes to GPU pools using a decision tree fed by network probes and GPU pool telemetry.
- Egress fencing: VPC-level policy that pins tenant traffic to allowed egress proxies and publishes fence status to the control plane.

2) High-level flow

- Periodic network probes (synthetic RPCs, HTTP pings) run across VPC egress nodes and report latency/p95 and loss to telemetry (prometheus + event bus).
- A routing controller ingests telemetry and tilts route weights between pools (same-region low-latency pool, fallback-burst pool, cold-pool) and selects an appropriate batching profile.
- Batching profile is pushed to the runtime via a signed config bundle stored in S3 and referenced by the route config.

Architecture diagram (text)

- Ingress API -> Routing Controller -> Model Router -> Serving Runtime (GPU pools)
  - Routing Controller queries Network Telemetry Store and Capacity API
  - Routing Controller emits decisions to Config Store (S3 + Consul)
  - Serving Runtime pulls profile from Config Store and applies batching live

IaC modules required

- network/egress-proxy-module: creates egress proxy fleet (autoscaling), NAT config, route tables, and health probe targets
- infra/batch-profile-store: S3 bucket policy, kms key, IAM roles for signing and retrieval
- infra/routing-controller-service: ECS/EKS deployment spec, service account, ALB, tracing and metrics exports
- compute/gpu-pool-module: GPU pool with node labels for latency tier, tenancy (dedicated/shared), and prewarming hooks
- iam/routing-roles: least-privilege roles allowing controller to read telemetry and write signed bundles

Example Terraform snippet (pseudo)

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "batch_profiles" {
  bucket = "redwood-batch-profiles-prod"
  acl    = "private"
}

module "gpu_pool_lowlatency" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood/internal-iac//modules/gpu-pool"
  name   = "gpu-pool-lowlatency-us-west-2"
  labels = { latency_tier = "low", placement = "us-west-2" }
  capacity = 50
}

module "egress_proxy" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood/internal-iac//modules/egress-proxy"
  name   = "egress-proxy-us-west-2"
  nat_config = { subnet_ids = var.private_subnets, egress_cidrs = var.egress_whitelist }
}

CI/CD and gating

- All changes to batching profiles, routing controller, and GPU pool node label logic must pass the following gates in the infra pipeline:
  1) Unit tests + static checks (tflint, checkov)
  2) Terraform plan with drift detection against staging environment
  3) Network simulation acceptance tests (see Simulation harness section)
  4) Canary deployment: controller rolled out to 10% of control-plane replicas and routes limited to non-production namespaces
  5) SLO validation run: synthetic probe validation and end-to-end latency smoke tests for 24h

- Example Buildkite steps (conceptual):
  - step: unit-tests
  - step: terraform-plan-staging
  - step: run-network-sims
  - step: canary-deploy-controller
  - step: monitor-slo-checks (manual approval if thresholds exceed)

Simulation harness (operational test)

- Purpose: ensure a new batching profile or routing change does not degrade tail latency under a variety of network conditions.
- Components: traffic-replay tool, packet-loss injector (tc/netem), latency shim that emulates cross-region RTT, GPU workload generator that produces model tokens with KV cache miss/hit patterns.
- Success criteria: 99th percentile end-to-end latency change <= +15% and no increase in error rate > 0.5% for the simulated tenant load.

Monitoring and SLOs

- Route-level SLOs to track:
  - p50/p95/p99 inference latency per route
  - error rate per route (5xx/timeout)
  - batch-apply latency (time from batch formation to dispatch)
  - egress-proxy p95 and packet loss

- Alerting thresholds (examples):
  - p95 latency > route_slo_p95 * 1.3 for 5 minutes -> P1 page to infra-oncall
  - error rate > 0.5% over 10 minutes -> P1 investigate (possible network partition)
  - config-signing failures or S3 retrieval failures -> P2 oncall

Operational runbook: incident response steps

1) Detection: automated alert or customer report indicating increased p99 latency.
2) Triage:
   - Query routing controller decision logs: which pool was selected for the affected route?
   - Check Network Telemetry dashboard for egress-proxy latency and packet loss spikes.
   - Confirm GPU pool capacity and node health (drains, OOMs).
3) Mitigation options (in order):
   - Re-route traffic to alternate same-region pool via the routing controller UI (manual override).
   - Reduce batch size for affected routes by pushing an emergency profile { max_batch: 4, max_wait_ms: 40 }.
   - Temporarily pin tenant route to dedicated pool to avoid noisy neighbor impacts.
4) Post-incident:
   - Run the Simulation harness to replay traffic and reproduce the symptom in staging.
   - Create a blameless incident review with root cause analysis and follow-up action items (link to page).

Rollback and upgrade strategy

- Controller and module changes follow a canary-first pattern. For config-only changes (batch profiles):
  - Deploy to staging bundle; run smoke tests; promote to canary (5% routes); validate for 60 minutes; promote to 20%; validate 4 hours; full rollout.
- If at any stage SLO regressions are detected, automated rollback policy will revert to the last signed bundle and trigger a Buildkite rollback job.

Security and compliance notes

- Batch profiles and routing decisions are stored in S3 encrypted with a dedicated KMS key. Access is constrained to the routing-controller service role and the audit-read role.
- All signed bundles include an HMAC and a short TTL (typically 1 hour) to avoid stale profile application during network partitions.
- Egress proxies must enforce allowed destination CIDRs per-tenant when required by customer contracts.

Ownership and contacts

- Routing controller service: inference-platform team (on call: inference-platform-oncall)
- Network egress and proxies: cloud-networking team
- GPU pool provisioning and labels: gpu-infra team

Appendix: Troubleshooting quick commands

- View last routing decisions (kubectl):
  kubectl logs deploy/routing-controller -n infra --since=1h | rg "decision" | jq -c '{route,decision}'

- Force push emergency profile to S3 (example):
  aws s3 cp emergency-profile.json s3://redwood-batch-profiles-prod//profiles/tenant-123.json --sse aws:kms

- Run local network sim (developer):
  tox -e network-sim -- --profile=high-loss --duration=10m

Document maintenance

- Owner: Maya Chen (inference-platform)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major routing or GPU fleet change

End of document
